title: Benchmark Report Launch: Field Deck Outline (AEs/SEs)
author: Markus Klein
body:
## Purpose
This page defines the *field deck storyline and slide-by-slide outline* for the public-facing “Production Economics: Latency per Dollar” benchmark report launch. The goal is to give AEs and SEs a repeatable narrative that:
- Explains *why* latency/$ matters (engineering + procurement framing).
- Establishes Redwood’s credibility via methodology (without over-claiming).
- Walks prospects through *how to interpret* results by model family and region.
- Converts interest into next steps (Hosted API trial, Dedicated sizing, Private/VPC evaluation).

**Primary users:** AEs, SEs, CS/Support (for consistent Q&A).

## When to use this deck
Use this deck for:
1) Inbound demo requests driven by the report/landing page.
2) Late-stage evaluations where performance/cost proof is requested.
3) Competitive bake-offs where a prospect asks “show me the numbers” across regions.

Do *not* use this deck as a generic Redwood overview in first meetings. Pair with the standard Redwood platform deck if the buyer is not yet aligned on inference vs model-layer decisions.

## Audience and meeting types
### A) Engineering-led evaluation (SE-heavy)
- Emphasize: methodology controls, repeatability, variance language, how to reproduce a subset.
- CTA: run a reproduction harness against their prompt set; share routing and capacity guidance.

### B) Procurement / platform leadership (AE-heavy)
- Emphasize: unit economics, predictability, dedicated capacity, SLAs, region coverage, governance.
- CTA: Dedicated sizing call + security package + pricing proposal.

### C) Regulated / EU data residency (mixed)
- Emphasize: region-specific tables, data residency posture, Private/VPC option, audit logs.
- CTA: security review + architecture session.

## Guardrails for external performance claims (must-follow)
Follow the rules in **Public Benchmarking Claims Guidelines**.
- Always say “in our benchmark” and name the workload profile.
- Do not claim universal superiority; do not generalize to all workloads.
- Use variance language when asked for absolutes (e.g., “we observed p95 within X–Y% across reruns”).
- If showing competitor comparisons, only show what is approved for the current report version and include the disclaimer slide.

## Core storyline (talk track)
1) **The new bottleneck is serving**: Teams don’t win by owning a model; they win by serving reliably and economically.
2) **Latency/$ aligns engineering + finance**: It captures user experience and cost efficiency in one metric.
3) **Benchmarks are often misleading**: Many omit region differences, caching/batching policies, and variance.
4) **Redwood benchmark = production economics**: Reproducible methodology, multiple regions, run-to-run QA.
5) **Actionable outcomes**: Use the report to pick region/model defaults, then tune with Redwood Optimize and operational tooling.
6) **Next step**: Reproduce a subset on the prospect’s workload and move to an implementation plan.

---

# Slide list (recommended 12–15 slides)
Below is the recommended deck flow. Slides marked **(optional)** can be added for longer meetings.

## 0. Title / opener
**Slide title:** Production Economics Benchmark: Latency per Dollar (LLM Inference)
- Subtitle: Model families × cloud regions
- Presenter: AE + SE

**Speaker notes:** Set expectations: “We’ll cover why latency/$ matters, how we measured it, what we found, and how you can reproduce it for your workload.”

## 1. Agenda
- Why latency/$
- Benchmark methodology (the parts that matter)
- Findings (by model family, by region)
- What this means for your workload
- Demo / reproduction path
- Next steps

## 2. Why teams care: user experience *and* unit economics
**Visual:** simple chart or two-axis framing (latency vs $)
- Latency impacts conversion / retention
- Cost per token impacts margin / CAC payback
- Reliability affects support burden and trust

**Speaker notes:** Bring it back to constraints: p95 latency, predictable spend, regional compliance.

## 3. Defining “Latency per Dollar” (clear + non-technical)
**Slide title:** Latency/$ = “How much latency you buy for $1” (lower is better)
- Computed from measured latency and metered cost
- Report shows p50 and p95 latency; primary comparisons use p95
- We also publish supporting throughput and cost metrics

**Required disclaimer (short):** “Results depend on workload profile; see methodology for details.”

## 4. What we measured (workloads)
- Chat baseline (streaming-compatible request pattern)
- Embeddings baseline (throughput-oriented)
- Fixed input distribution and concurrency policy

**Speaker notes:** Emphasize this is not “max tokens at all costs”; it’s “production-like distribution and concurrency.”

## 5. Methodology credibility: controls and repeatability
**Slide title:** We controlled the variables that usually invalidate benchmarks
Include bullets:
- Warmup policy and steady-state measurement windows
- Caching/batching policy declared and consistent
- Region-specific runs with the same harness and config
- Rerun policy on variance thresholds + anomaly triage
- Results are aggregated with QA sign-off

**Speaker notes:** This slide is the “trust wedge.” Spend time here if challenged.

## 6. Coverage: models and regions
**Slide title:** Coverage in this report
- Models: curated, high-demand open families (see appendix for exact list)
- Regions: NA + EU + APAC coverage (report shows per-region tables)
- Refresh cadence: planned periodic updates (avoid implying real-time)

**Optional:** “How to request a model/region to be added” (internal process + customer path)

## 7. Headline findings (approved language only)
**Slide title:** What we observed (high level)
- Latency/$ varies materially by region and model family
- Some models are cost-efficient but have higher p95; others trade cost for tail latency
- Region selection can be as important as model selection for p95 experience

**Speaker notes:** Keep this “directional + actionable” and avoid superlatives.

## 8. Findings: by model family (chart 1)
**Slide title:** Latency/$ by model family (region-normalized view)
**Visual:** bar or scatter (family on x-axis; latency/$ on y)
- Annotate “chat” vs “embeddings” if separate charts

**Speaker notes:** Provide a short interpretation: “This family tends to optimize for X; if your workload is Y, start here.”

## 9. Findings: by region (chart 2)
**Slide title:** Latency/$ by region (same model/config)
**Visual:** matrix or small multiples
- Callouts for NA/EU/APAC differences

**Speaker notes:** Tie to buyer reality: data residency, user geography, multi-region failover.

## 10. How to use this report (decision framework)
**Slide title:** Turning charts into a deployment decision
A simple 3-step flow:
1) Pick region(s) based on user distribution + residency
2) Pick model family based on quality target and tail-latency needs
3) Tune runtime levers (batching/caching/quantization) with Redwood Optimize

**Speaker notes:** Position Redwood as the system that keeps this consistent across hosted/dedicated/private.

## 11. Redwood product tie-in (without “feature dump”)
**Slide title:** Why this is hard to operationalize without an inference platform
- Consistent runtime across deployment modes
- Observability: token-level cost + latency breakdown
- Rollouts + fallback policies
- Dedicated capacity for predictable throughput

**Speaker notes:** Connect capabilities to benchmark risks (variance, tail latency, cost drift, regional capacity).

## 12. Demo flow (SE-led): “Reproduce a subset”
**Slide title:** Reproduce a subset in 15 minutes (customer-safe)
**Goal:** Show the prospect *how they can validate results* on their prompts.

**Demo steps (high level):**
1) Pick a region + model from the report
2) Run the reproduction harness on a small prompt set
3) Show output: latency distribution + cost + derived latency/$
4) Show how changing concurrency or max tokens shifts p95 and cost

**Speaker notes:** Be explicit: “This is a subset, not a carbon copy of the full benchmark suite.”

## 13. Pricing tie-in and “what you do next”
**Slide title:** Next steps (choose one)
- Hosted API: start with $X credits + recommended defaults (region + model)
- Dedicated: sizing session (throughput target, p95 SLO, region)
- Private/VPC: architecture and security review

**Speaker notes:** Avoid quoting specific prices on the slide unless regionally approved; direct to pricing discussion and internal calculator.

## 14. Objections and FAQ (optional, for longer meetings)
- “Benchmarks don’t reflect my workload” → reproduction path + offer a joint run
- “Why is my region performance different?” → routing policy, time-of-day, network path, workload shape
- “Are you optimizing only for the benchmark?” → controls + guardrails + published methodology
- “Can I see raw logs?” → no; sanitized aggregates + reproducibility guide

## 15. Closing slide
**Slide title:** Validate production economics on your workload
- CTA: book reproduction session / sizing call
- Links: report landing page + methodology appendix

---

# Demo / reproduction runbook (speaker-ready)
**Owner:** SE (Markus Klein + regional SE)

## Preconditions
- Confirm region selection mechanism (headers/params) for the prospect’s integration style.
- Use a customer-safe prompt set (no proprietary data unless prospect provides and approves).
- Confirm rate limits / quotas for demo key.

## Suggested live demo sequence (10–15 min)
1) Start with report’s recommended default (one model, one region).
2) Run ~50–200 requests (small but enough to show p95 behavior).
3) Show:
   - p50/p95 latency
   - tokens/sec or throughput
   - cost per 1M tokens (or normalized unit)
   - derived latency/$
4) Change one knob (concurrency or output tokens) and rerun.
5) Close with “production checklist”: routing, fallbacks, and dedicated capacity if needed.

## Fallback plan (if live run fails)
- Use pre-generated artifacts captured during internal benchmark windows (approved screenshots only).
- State clearly they are from the benchmark environment and offer to rerun later.

---

# Appendix (slides to include at end)
## A1. Methodology summary (one slide)
- Workload definitions
- Concurrency and distribution
- Warmup/steady-state window
- Caching/batching policy
- Variance + rerun criteria

## A2. Full region table
- Table format: Region name, short code, notes on availability (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
- Include: NA/EU/APAC entries present in the report

## A3. Model catalog mapping
- Model family → specific version(s) used
- Note: “Results apply to the versions tested; newer versions may differ.”

## A4. Metric definitions
- p50 vs p95
- Throughput definition
- Cost metric definition
- Latency/$ derivation (simple formula form)

## A5. Claims and disclaimers (required)
Include as a standard slide for sharing externally:
- “In our benchmark, under the workload described…"
- “Do not generalize results beyond the measured configuration.”
- “Comparisons are only for the models/regions tested and reported.”

## A6. Pricing and packaging tie-in (internal-only variant)
**Note:** Keep this slide in the *internal-only* deck version.
- Hosted API pricing structure (high level)
- Dedicated commit mechanics (how capacity maps to throughput targets)
- Private licensing + support tiers (high level)

---

# Versioning and distribution
- **Deck file name convention:** Benchmark_Report_FieldDeck_v{major}.{minor}_YYYY-MM-DD
- **Public-sharing rule:** Only share the externally-approved PDF export with disclaimers slide included.
- **Internal-sharing rule:** Internal-only version may include pricing tie-in appendix.

# Owners and update cadence
- **Content owner:** Jordan Blake (Sales) + Soojin Lee (Messaging)
- **Technical owner:** Markus Klein (SE) + Jonas Weber (Methodology)
